summary: This standards-track document defines how to run NETCONF inside a Secure Shell session as an SSH subsystem. SSH supplies authentication and protection for the configuration messages. It replaces RFC 4742.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6242 explains how to run NETCONF inside an SSH session. It also defines length-based framing for peers that both support the newer NETCONF base capability.

questions: what port does netconf over ssh use
what is the netconf ssh subsystem
subtitle: A NETCONF SSH subsystem with negotiated message framing and a default TCP port of 830.

tldr.problem: NETCONF needs a transport mapping that protects configuration traffic and separates complete XML messages. The earlier delimiter could legally occur inside XML.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens an SSH session and invokes the netconf subsystem. After hello messages, peers that both advertise base:1.1 use chunk framing with an explicit size for each chunk.
tldr.outcome: SSH provides authentication and encryption for the session. RFC 6242 obsoletes RFC 4742.

today: RFC 6242 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4742. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 6242.

sections.title: NETCONF over an SSH Session
sections.content:
NETCONF is an XML-based protocol for managing network equipment. RFC 6242 maps NETCONF onto an SSH session so clients and servers can exchange any NETCONF messages through that transport.

The SSH transport protects the channel, while this document specifies how NETCONF is invoked and how its messages are framed.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF carries XML messages for managing network equipment. This RFC explains how those messages travel inside an SSH session.

sections.title: Starting the NETCONF Subsystem
sections.content:
The SSH client establishes the transport, exchanges keys for integrity and encryption, authenticates the user, and opens a session channel. It then invokes an SSH subsystem named netconf.

Servers MUST offer this subsystem by default on TCP port 830, and SHOULD allow configuration for other ports. The SSH username is passed to NETCONF unchanged; if it cannot be represented in XML, the session must be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first establishes and authenticates SSH, then requests the subsystem named netconf. The default TCP port is 830.

sections.title: Exchanging Capabilities
sections.content:
Once the subsystem starts, both peers send an XML <hello> document listing capabilities. They may send these documents at the same time.

After the hello exchange, the client sends complete XML documents containing <rpc> elements and the server replies with <rpc-reply> documents. The shared base:1.1 capability selects the newer framing method.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side sends a hello document that lists supported features. Those capability lists determine how the rest of the messages are separated.

sections.title: Chunked Message Framing
sections.content:
The former separator ]]>]]> can appear legally inside XML attributes, comments, and processing instructions. The new framing is used after hello when both peers advertise base:1.1.

A message contains one or more chunks. Each starts with a line feed, a hash sign, a decimal length, and another line feed; that many octets follow. A line feed, two hash signs, and another line feed end the chunks. The maximum chunk length is 4294967295, and invalid framing requires the peer to close the SSH channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk states how many octets follow, so the receiver counts message data instead of searching for a delimiter. Both peers must advertise base:1.1 to use this method.

sections.title: The Older End Marker
sections.content:
For compatibility, peers use end-of-message framing when the other peer supports only base:1.0. In that mode, each complete XML document is followed by ]]>]]>.

The hello document also uses this marker before the peers choose which framing applies for the rest of the session.
sections.plainLanguage: Older peers use the original marker after each XML document. The hello exchange uses that marker so both sides can select the framing they share.

sections.title: Closing the Session
sections.content:
A client closes NETCONF by sending the <close-session> operation. The server processes messages in arrival order, sends its response, and closes the SSH session channel.

The server MUST NOT process messages received after it processes close-session.
sections.plainLanguage: After close-session, the server replies and closes the channel. It must ignore later NETCONF messages on that session.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NETCONF can expose and change configuration, including sensitive values. The SSH client must verify the server identity before sending credentials or configuration data, and the server must verify the client before exchanging configuration data.

Chunked framing avoids the delimiter ambiguity after hello. The fixed default port makes traffic easier to filter and also easier to identify; changing ports without corresponding firewall changes can expose access unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must verify the identity of the other before exchanging configuration information. Administrators should also keep firewall rules aligned with the port where NETCONF is available.
